approachQuestion.prompt:
A read-only array contains one unsigned identifier once and every other distinct identifier exactly three times. Return the once-occurring identifier.

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 200000; all identifiers use exactly 32 bits, including the high bit.
Example: [6,6,11,6] -> 11. Edge case: [4294967295] -> 4294967295.

Choose the best approach under these constraints.
constraints: Unsigned 32-bit shifts and bitwise operations cost constant time. The width 32 is fixed, not a size parameter.
Inputs are read-only. Include all temporary storage and any call stack; exclude the supplied input and the returned output. No input copy is implicit.

options.text: For each of the 32 positions, count input words having that bit set; set the result bit when the count modulo three is one.
options.feedback: Tripled identifiers contribute a multiple of three at each position. The remainder reconstructs every bit of the single identifier.

options.text: Sort a copy and find the run of length one.
options.feedback: All legal runs have length three except one, so this is correct, but sorting and copying are avoidable.

options.text: XOR all identifiers and return the result.
options.feedback: An odd triple does not vanish under XOR. [6,6,11,6] produces 13 instead of 11.

options.text: Return the integer average of all identifiers.
options.feedback: The multiplicities do not make the mean equal to the single value: [6,6,11,6] averages to 7 after truncation, not 11.

feedback.reason: At each bit, triplicated values contribute multiples of three and vanish modulo three.
details: Visit all 32 bit positions. At each position count the set bits across the input and reduce the count modulo three. Reconstruct the answer from those remainders, using unsigned operations even at position 31.

At each bit, triplicated values contribute multiples of three and vanish modulo three. Reconstruct every bit of the singleton, including bit 31 with unsigned semantics. Ordinary XOR would not cancel triples.

“For each of the 32 positions, count input words having that bit set; set the result bit when the count modulo three is one.”: Tripled identifiers contribute a multiple of three at each position. The remainder reconstructs every bit of the single identifier.
“Sort a copy and find the run of length one.”: All legal runs have length three except one, so this is correct, but sorting and copying are avoidable.
“XOR all identifiers and return the result.”: An odd triple does not vanish under XOR. [6,6,11,6] produces 13 instead of 11.
“Return the integer average of all identifiers.”: The multiplicities do not make the mean equal to the single value: [6,6,11,6] averages to 7 after truncation, not 11.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For count-each-bit-mod-three, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the number of words; 32 is a fixed constant.
constraints: Unsigned 32-bit shifts and bitwise operations cost constant time. The width 32 is fixed, not a size parameter.
Inputs are read-only. Include all temporary storage and any call stack; exclude the supplied input and the returned output. No input copy is implicit.

feedback.reason: Exactly 32 scans are linear in input length with fixed word state.
details: There are 32 input scans. One count, position, index and result suffice; a table of identifiers is unnecessary.
Unsigned 32-bit shifts and bitwise operations cost constant time. The width 32 is fixed, not a size parameter.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The analyzed method does not retain a table or copy.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This is looser than the bounded number of scans.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The input cannot be processed without scanning it in the worst case.
